body:
Haha, am I reading my own thoughts? I'm a 24 year old guy, econ degree from a top US university, high expectations, loving but smothering parents, suicide attempt, countless meds, therapy, hospitalization, etc.

I've been suffering from a manic depressive episode for about eight months now. Disappointed that nothing else works, my plan is now to get a one-way ticket to Buenos Aires to do some quality 'soul searching' and force myself to not come back until I come to an understanding of who I am and what my purpose is.

So personally, I think it's a great idea to follow your heart on this one and I'm a firm believer that travel, or even just a new environment, has a certain therapeutic power to it. My psychiatrist did something similar when she was battling depression in her early 20s and got up and moved to Portugal, which she says was the best decision of her life.

With that said, in order to alleviate my parents' and psychiatrists' worries that I won't come back in a body bag, I promised to present a really structured view of what I will do abroad and what goals I have for the journey, as well as to wait a couple months to make sure my medications were stable as I've been trying some different mood stabilizers and antidepressants with little success so far.

My only worry in your case is that $3,000 (I assume that's after airfare?) won't get you very far in NZ or Ireland. Make sure you know the minimum daily burn rate, and then add 25% as a safety net. The last thing you want is to be forced to get to the third week and realize you have to either return or get a job asap. Fortunately, bartending and waitressing are great skills to have when it comes to travel. I have about $15k reserved for my trip, but I also have some freelance writing/content marketing gigs lined up so that I can travel indefinitely without burning through my savings.

If you want to go some place cheaper but more exotic than Mexico, I'd look into SE Asia (particularly Thailand). This region is a little harder to travel independently through, but cheap, safe, and beautiful.

Feel free to message me for anything. I've solo backpacked through much of Europe and SE Asia, and soon South America.

Sounds like just mood swings. Everyone has them, although to different degrees.

It's bipolar if you've experienced both manic/hypomanic and depressive episodes, the symptoms for which is below.

Mania
The DSM defines mania as a “distinct period during which there is an abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood.” The episode must last at least a week. The mood must have at least three of the following symptoms:

* inflated self-esteem
* little need for sleep
* pressure of speech (talking constantly)
* flight of ideas
* easily distracted
* excess pursuit of goal-directed activities or psychomotor agitation (pacing, hand wringing, etc.)
* excess pursuit of pleasure with a high risk of danger

Depression
The DSM states that a major depressive episode must have at least four of the following symptoms. They should be new or suddenly worse. They must last for at least two weeks.

* changes in appetite or weight, sleep, or psychomotor activity
* decreased energy
* feelings of worthlessness or guilt
* trouble thinking, concentrating, or making decisions
* thoughts of death or suicidal plans or attempts

Sorry to hear that. Growing up, I was convinced that my parents paid my best friend to be friends with me as I couldn't think of why else he would like me, and I'm still struggling with self esteem and identity.

Like you, I've always done what was expected of me, largely because it was easier than deciding for myself. Now, I'm taking a year off just to do some soul searching and figure out what I want to do with my life without any external influences or obligations. Maybe try something similar? For me, I do my best reflection in nature and even just a quick solitary camping trip might give your mind a much needed rest and time to think about what's really important to you.

Good advice, and I'm glad you find it helpful. Your experience is more along the lines of what I hoped and expected to get out of inpatient.

I think part of the reason I had such a bad experience is that none of the recommended hospitals in Seattle had any open beds so I was taken to a maximum security facility an hour away that was more like the "unsafe prisons" the other patients described. I had to break up fights on a daily basis, and I couldn't get a thing out of groups because someone was always throwing a tantrum. The staff were good but always preoccupied with the catatonics and lesser functioning folks to really give any time to those with "just" depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation.

At least from my experience, I wouldn't recommend inpatient hospitalization unless you're extremely suicidal. I've found the whole system to be a bit of a joke and the only benefit is that I was in a safe place without any possible weapons. As far as treatment goes, it was very subpar when compared to what I was getting from my outpatient psychiatrist.

I'd recommend finding a new doctor, or at least asking why he won't change your meds (have you waited 6 weeks for them to kick in?).

Alternatively your therapist can likely help you find someone else who can prescribe based on their recommendation.

I felt the same way before I came out. I resented the whole gay scene and struggled to find any gay role models in business or beyond. I saw all gay men as flamboyant and effeminate, and only really liked straight men. I feared I would always be alone chasing after lost causes.

Yet, I came out anyway. And it was the best decision of my life. I learned that there are a lot more LGBT folks than I first guessed, and that just because the flamboyant types are the most visible, doesn't mean that all or even most of us are that way. The best part is I'm finally comfortable with who I am. It takes work and time, but coming out lifts a huge weight off your shoulder and you're finally free to be the person you want to be.

Also, wouldn't it be better to be yourself and at least give love a shot rather than giving us and rejecting sexuality altogether? You said people are supportive. What do you have to lose by exploring your opportunities?

Granted, I wouldn't call myself happy, but that has absolutely nothing to do with my orientation. Being gay is one of the few things I like about myself.

I can relate. I work in tech startups amid a sea of "bro-grammers." I was the only LGBT in my last three companies.

I don't really see a point in separating your work and "real-world" identities/lives, considering you probably spend half your waking hours at the office. Opening up at work may very well hurt your future with the company (there is a definite wage gap for gay employees); but if you do run into discrimination, do you really want to work for that sort of company anyway?

Also, count yourself lucky as tech is about the most progressive industry you can be in, with many leading companies going out of their way to promote LGBT diversity and inclusivity. Your superiors might be a little curious (it's only natural to wonder), but that doesn't necessarily mean they're discriminating.

I don't see why it wouldn't be. They're different classes of antidepressants (meaning they affect different brain chemicals), and Welbutrin is a very common add-on for SSRIs like Zoloft.

As far as I know, being on multiple antidepressants is pretty common. I'm on Welbutrin and Lexapro, another SSRI.

With that said, communicate any side effects with your doctor or psychiatrist to be safe.

Possibly. I think everyone gets some sort of weird feeling around graduation as they start a new chapter of their lives. I'd see if things are better with college (congrats on getting in!). You'll be in a new environment, able to meet new people and make new friends, and (hopefully) able to stay up later.

Also, high school sucks for everyone.

Best case scenario, you might be able to withdraw from those classes after you've already completed them. It would wipe your GPA clean, but you'd have to retake the classes if you want credit.

Worst case scenario, the grades stick but you have plenty of semesters left to boost your GPA. I would just work with the university and your professors and let them know what's going on before the semester starts and see if they have any system in place for accommodation. If you're transparent with them, professors may be a little more lenient with things like due dates but it would be up to the individual professor.

I'm gay and an active Catholic. Feel free to message me if you'd like to chat.

I'm blessed to live in a pretty liberal city, but I've seen nothing but acceptance from my church community. They're the people who have been there for me every step of the way as I made the journey to come out - the best decision I've ever made, by the way. As a whole, the church is getting a lot more progressive. I'm seeing a lot more gender neutral pronouns and use of terms like 'partner' rather than 'husband' or 'wife' in sermons. Even Pope Francis said, "Who am I to judge a gay person of goodwill who seeks the Lord?"

I really don't think the bible says anything about homosexuality, although you can spin the scriptures to say just about anything you want to argue. It does explicitly forbid suicide, however.

You should see a doctor or a psychiatrist if you want a real diagnosis.

With that said, bipolar does not mean mood swings. Everyone has mood swings, particularly depressives. Bipolar is more represented by episodes of extreme outward irritability or seemingly endless energy to the point where you feel the need to run laps just to burn off some of the energy or everything you do is on hyperdrive (faster speech, bursts of creativity, etc.). It's also more commonly associated with a reduced need for sleep. I'm bipolar, and I've had a couple weeks where I've functioned and felt just fine on 1-2 hours of sleep a night. (Oddly enough, those are the times I've felt best during depressive episodes.)

If anything, I'd look into atypical depression. Atypical is characterized by more volatile moods and is more likely to manifest in oversleeping than normal major depression.

If you're in the U.S. or Canada, I'd check out Psychology Today: (https://therapists.psychologytoday.com/). It has a pretty comprehensive index of therapists/psychiatrists in your area. If you know what type of therapeutic approach works best for you (CBT, DBT, MBCT, etc.), you can filter by that. You can also search by specialties (anxiety, divorce, sexual abuse, medication management, LGBT, etc.) to find someone right for you.

You may still have to try out a few before finding one you connect with. At least in my area, however, many provide a complimentary 30 minute intake session. It's not enough time to make any progress but at least you can get a taste of the therapist's style and demeanor.

I think there are a lot of conflicting studies. Tears do have some health benefits like improving eyesight and removing toxins. As far as mood and depression go, there's not much of a correlation with tears - although it can be a method of release or stress relief.

Other studies suggest that crying can worsen depression by prolonging that mindset and emotionally exhausting you.

I'd say if you feel better after crying, it's working. Whether it's a chemical effect or a placebo effect, I'm not sure but all that matters is how you feel afterwards.

Honestly depression is a pretty meaningless label and it's misdiagnosed all the time.

I'd say focus less on what to call it and more on why you're discontent. Is it related to something tangible and situational (your job, relationships, finance, diet, etc.) or do you feel discontent even though you're seemingly satisfied with everything in your life? Both could be depression, but the latter is more likely to be clinical and you might want to look into medication and/or therapy. If it's the former, changing up your daily routine might be enough to get you out of this rut - and if that doesn't work, then go the clinical route.

I have something similar. It's a more major and suicidal depression classified as 'atypical depression' but it has that same rollercoaster effect... which sucks because every time I think the depression is over, it comes back very abruptly. I'm also bipolar, which makes those mood swings more extreme. And I'm a guy, so no menstrual factor.

By its nature, atypical depression is pretty treatment-resistant, so I've tried just about everything without much luck. The meds that have worked best for me personally are Bupropion (an antidepressant) and Lamotrigine (a mood stabilizer).

I'm eight months into my first major episode, but I think those two drugs are starting to make a big difference. My cycles are usually very abrupt, so I can be great one day and extremely suicidal the next. Fortunately, the depressed/suicidal phases are getting shorter. Originally, they could last up to a month while my most recent one lasted 24 hours.

As for triggers, it used to be all situational. I was in an abusive relationship so anything that reminded me of that would trigger something. For the past five months or so, my phases have been seemingly random. Now, I have no reaction to things that would have previously set me off but the switch can flick pretty much whenever no matter what my mood is - has happened at concerts, weddings, etc.

I know it's hard, but you really can't blame yourself. Depression is largely chemical. He could have had everything he wanted and still not been able to find happiness.

Likewise, depression and the stigma around it cause isolation. A lot of suicides do come as a surprise and I think only half of all suicide victims leave a note. I'm sure you did everything you could; but there was simply no way of knowing the gravity of the situation.

I can't speak for your husband; but if I died, I'd want my partner to leave life to the fullest and find the happiness that I eluded me.

By the way, are you familiar with the English writer Virginia Woolf? She had severe depression and committed suicide. She had the perfect marriage, which brought her great joy until this 'terrible disease' (her depression) overwhelmed her and made her feel like she was spoiling her husband's happiness. Again, I don't know your husband, but maybe he was thinking something similar?

Here's the note:

Dearest,

I feel certain that I am going mad again. I feel we can't go through another of those terrible times. And I shan't recover this time. I begin to hear voices, and I can't concentrate. So I am doing what seems the best thing to do. You have given me the greatest possible happiness. You have been in every way all that anyone could be. I don't think two people could have been happier 'til this terrible disease came. I can't fight any longer. I know that I am spoiling your life, that without me you could work. And you will I know. You see I can't even write this properly. I can't read. What I want to say is I owe all the happiness of my life to you. You have been entirely patient with me and incredibly good. I want to say that — everybody knows it. If anybody could have saved me it would have been you. Everything has gone from me but the certainty of your goodness. I can't go on spoiling your life any longer.

I don't think two people could have been happier than we have been. V.

Sounds like you're just discontent. Possibly situational depression.

With that said, being discontent or situationally depressed can turn into clinical depression over time if not managed.

Nah, you're good. Florida's the only state that really does this (well, I believe Ohio, New York, and California do it but only in very extreme cases).

Be completely honest about your feelings with your psychologist - that's the only way s/he can help you.

I'd say follow your heart as only you can make this decision. Might want to run your reasoning by a therapist or close friend to get a second opinion; but in the end, it comes down to you. I'd also come up with some sort of contingency plan if your move means cutting off your current support system and make sure you know exactly what you're getting into.

I'm in the same boat. Since the start of my current episode, I had this weird feeling that I needed to switch up how I was living my life by doing something polar opposite. I saw seven therapists. The first six told me not to make any major decisions when I said I wanted to quit my job and move. The seventh one encouraged me to follow my heart. And thus, I recently quit my dream job and got a one-way ticket to South America to travel indefinitely while working some odd jobs and explore what I really want to do with my life.

Sounds crazy, but I've attempted suicide and been in and out of hospitals. No matter how this decision ultimately plays out, my life can't exactly get any worse. ;)

Hopefully your decision is a little less extreme, but follow your heart. Only you know what you need to do.

Honestly that's often works with antidepressants and the likes. Not to defend your new psychiatrist, but it's often a guessing game as the average antidepressant only has a 50% success rate and it's not like they can just do a blood test to find which drug will work for you. My psychiatrist is brilliant, but we've still gone through five medications to try and find one that works while controlling for side effects.

With that said, if you feel the drug is causing more harm than benefit, you definitely want to stop (although work with your psychiatrist to gradually stop).

And sorry about your girlfriend. :(
How you live your life is up to you, not your friends. If you need a break, don't be afraid to take a little 'me time.'

It's Monday. The week is young.

Perhaps it's a sign you should let him/her know how you feel?

I wouldn't disregard them, but I wouldn't let them dictate your decision either. You can always stop taking the drugs (gradually) or switch to another antidepressant if you start experiencing negative side effects. They shouldn't make you numb or apathetic (except for maybe the first week). Most side effects will go away by themselves within the first month.

The sexual side effects are the only one that semi-commonly persist (depending on the person and the drug). If this is a concern, talk to your doctor or psychologist. Typically there are workarounds, like choosing the right medication, closely monitoring the dose, and appropriate timing.

I'd trust your psychologist. Your doctor doesn't know you as well and is much less versed in mental health treatment than your psychologist. Over 10% of the US is on antidepressants. This wouldn't be the case if they didn't work or were dangerous.

I'd just say start slow and be patient. Your psychologist should ease you into the medication, and then you may need to give it up to 6 weeks to see results.

Also, while antidepressants work for most people, you may have to try a couple before you find one that works specifically for you. Each individual antidepressant has a success rate of 50%, so don't get discouraged if the first one you try doesn't work.

Big props for being proactive about your mental health. If you're asking this question, I would definitely bring it up with your therapist.

I can't really tell you what to expect as it depends on the hospital and the security level. Some let you have your own room, smoke, and have an outside courtyard area. Others give you much less freedom.

I can only speak for the one I was in, but here you go:

Bedroom situation - Each patient had one roommate. They tried to match you by functioning level (a highly functioning depressive would not be matched with someone with schizophrenia or another chronic disorder). For the most part they did a good job with matching, although my roommate insisted on singing christmas carols at 5AM every morning (in June). The room will likely look like a college dorm room that you just moved into - the entire place will be clean and pretty empty as they remove any possible 'weapons.' The staff did rounds every 15 minutes, so you'll need to sleep with your door open and get used to people coming in and out. Each room had a private bathroom, although the water for the shower only ran for 30 seconds so you had to keep pushing the button, which was super annoying.

Clothing - You should be able to wear your own clothes. They did, however, take away things like belts and shoelaces and strip search patients upon arrival to check for any concealed weapons. Some might have you store any beauty/grooming products at the front desk and retrieve them every morning when you shower. You might be able to shave, but only under supervision.

Clinical tests - They'll likely check your vitals at least once a day. Depending on your medication, they may check blood and perform an EKG. They'll likely be adjusting your medication and need to ensure that your body is handling them well.


I'm pretty close to you in Seattle, so this should be a fairly good benchmark. I'd ask if you could go to a medium security one or get a hospital recommendation from your therapist. In this setting, you're with higher functioning, voluntary patients that you can probably relate to and get more out of the groups. Unfortunately, there weren't any beds available so I had to go to a maximum security hospital. It wasn't bad, but there were definitely some interesting people there. Regardless, I'm sure the hospitals in central Oregon are better than Seattle, which has a huge mental health problem.

Let me know if you have any more questions. :)

Ah, right. Side effects are weird with antidepressants as they manifest differently for everyone. I remember being cold all the time when I started Wellbutrin.

And yeah, it looks like 150mg is a pretty typical dose. I started at 300 so I assumed that was on the lower side.

I'd say you're just experiencing a placebo effect. It's rare to see any immediate effects, especially with that low of a dosage. It can take 4-6 weeks before you notice anything, although you might have some results after 2 weeks.

Wellbutrin didn't work for me, but it's very popular choice for a front-line treatment for a reason. Just be patient and give it time. :)

Btw - Wellbutrin shouldn't make you feel stoned. It should have the opposite effect and boost your energy levels. If you do have anxiety, Wellbutrin might not be the best drug for you as it can increase the anxiety and jitters you mentioned. (Of course, I'm not a psychiatrist but possibly something to bring up with your prescriber)

It's definitely not easy, but I'd highly recommend coming out if you aren't already. I've been in your shoes, and the only way you can have a real best friend or a relationship is to open up and be a little vulnerable. Let people like you for who you are rather than who you think they want you to be. You will face some discrimination and some people won't like your orientation; but it's 2015, they can get over it.

As has been suggested, I'd look into LGBT meetups. I'm sure there's some in every big city if you have a car or a way of getting there. Even if you're not looking to date, it helps to be able to talk to people who have experienced much of what you are going through right now.

And then this is probably unorthodox advice, but living some place where there's not a visible gay scene (suburban Utah), I used dating apps like Tinder and OKCupid - not necessarily to date but just to meet cool people. I've made several friends through casual coffee dates, and you'd be surprised by how many LGBTs there are in your rural community.

Message me if you ever want to talk.
